subtopic_detail: Treatment choice when attention symptoms and a chronic tic disorder coexist in a school aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric psychiatry registrar. A 9 year old boy has been assessed as meeting criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with impairment at school and at home documented on teacher and parent rating scales.

For the past two years he has also had bouts of eye blinking and shoulder shrugging, and for the last eight months a repeated throat clearing sound. His mother says these wax and wane, are worse when he is tired or anxious, and that he can hold them back briefly at the cost of building tension. He is teased about the throat clearing. His growth, cardiovascular examination and sleep are normal, and there is no family history of sudden cardiac death. His mother has read that stimulants cause tics and does not want him to have one.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 104/64, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Intermittent eye blinking and shoulder shrugs during interview, audible throat clearing, normal cardiovascular examination, height and weight on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Teacher and parent rating scales in the clinical range for inattention and hyperactivity; electrocardiogram not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start guanfacine and provide behavioural intervention with review of both sets of symptoms
options.rationale: An alpha 2 adrenergic agonist treats the attention symptoms and reduces tic frequency at the same time, which suits a child whose two conditions coexist and whose mother declines a stimulant (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP: ADHD).

options.text: Start risperidone to suppress the tics and defer any treatment of the attention symptoms
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do suppress tics but carry weight gain, metabolic and movement risks and are reserved for severe tics after other options, while leaving the functional impairment untreated (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Provide behavioural intervention alone and review both sets of symptoms in six months
options.rationale: Behavioural therapy is a genuine component and comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics works well, but documented impairment at school and home warrants treatment of the attention symptoms too (Source: RANZCP: ADHD).

options.text: Start atomoxetine and refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics as well
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is a reasonable non stimulant choice that is tic neutral, but it lacks the direct tic reducing effect of an alpha 2 agonist in a child with both conditions (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Start methylphenidate at a low dose and stop it immediately if any tics become worse
options.rationale: Stimulants are not contraindicated by tics and trial data show no consistent worsening, but starting one against a clear parental objection undermines the adherence the treatment depends on (Source: RANZCP: ADHD).

explanation.summary: Chronic tic disorder and Tourette syndrome coexist with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in a large proportion of affected children, and in most cases the attention symptoms cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves. The long standing teaching that stimulants cause or worsen tics has not been borne out by randomised evidence, and stimulants remain usable where tics coexist, but where a family is reluctant or the tics are themselves troubling, an alpha 2 adrenergic agonist such as guanfacine or clonidine treats both problems with a single agent. Tics characteristically wax and wane, are preceded by a premonitory urge, can be suppressed briefly at the cost of mounting tension, and worsen with fatigue and anxiety, all of which distinguishes them from stereotypies or seizures. Antipsychotics are effective tic suppressants but their metabolic and extrapyramidal burden confines them to severe or refractory cases.
key_points: Attention symptoms usually cause more impairment than the tics themselves
Alpha 2 agonists treat both attention symptoms and tics with one agent
Randomised evidence does not support stimulants causing or worsening tics
Premonitory urge with brief suppressibility identifies a tic rather than a stereotypy
Antipsychotics are reserved for severe or refractory tics
explanation.pearls: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics teaches a competing response to the premonitory urge and matches antipsychotic efficacy for mild to moderate tics without any metabolic cost.

subtopic_detail: Dosing strategy for a serotonergic antidepressant in cyclical premenstrual mood symptoms
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 31 year old woman describes irritability, tearfulness and a sense of being out of control that starts about six days before each period and lifts within two days of bleeding starting. She has snapped at her children and nearly resigned from her job during these episodes.

She has kept a daily symptom chart for three consecutive cycles which shows a clear symptom free interval from day 4 to day 16 of each cycle. Her cycles are regular at 28 days. She has no depressive or anxiety symptoms outside the premenstrual window, no history of a depressive episode and no thyroid disease. She uses condoms for contraception and does not want to start a hormonal method.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic and reactive on the day of review, which is day 9 of her cycle, with normal mental state examination
data_table.Investigations: Three cycles of prospective daily symptom rating showing a symptom free follicular phase; thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Prescribe a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken only from ovulation until menstruation starts
options.rationale: Luteal phase only dosing is as effective as continuous treatment in this condition because the response is rapid rather than taking weeks, and it halves total drug exposure (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously every day of the cycle instead
options.rationale: Continuous dosing is equally effective and is preferred when symptoms extend outside the luteal phase or cycles are irregular, neither of which applies to her charted pattern (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Prescribe oral micronised progesterone during the luteal phase of each menstrual cycle
options.rationale: Luteal progesterone has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo in this condition and can itself provoke the mood symptoms in susceptible women (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome).

options.text: Prescribe a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back oestrogen and progestogen
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression is effective but is a late line option because of bone loss and menopausal symptoms, used only after serotonergic and hormonal treatments have failed (Source: RANZCOG: Premenstrual Syndrome).

options.text: Prescribe a low dose benzodiazepine taken as required during the premenstrual week only
options.rationale: Intermittent anxiolytics blunt the irritability but carry dependence risk with repeated monthly use and are not a first line treatment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder is diagnosed on at least two cycles of prospective daily symptom ratings showing marked mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase with a symptom free follicular interval, which is what separates it from a mood or anxiety disorder that simply worsens premenstrually. Serotonergic antidepressants are first line and work quite differently here from their use in depression, producing benefit within a day or two through a neurosteroid mediated mechanism rather than over weeks. That rapid onset is what makes luteal phase only dosing possible, given from ovulation until menstruation begins, with efficacy equal to continuous treatment and roughly half the drug exposure and adverse effect burden. Continuous dosing is preferred when cycles are irregular, when symptoms spill outside the luteal phase, or when a coexisting depressive or anxiety disorder is present.
key_points: Prospective daily charting over at least two cycles is required for the diagnosis
A genuinely symptom free follicular phase separates it from premenstrual exacerbation
Serotonergic antidepressants act within days in this condition, not weeks
Luteal phase only dosing matches continuous dosing for efficacy
Ovarian suppression is a late line option because of bone and menopausal effects
explanation.pearls: Because the response is rapid rather than cumulative, discontinuation symptoms are uncommon when a serotonergic antidepressant used only in the luteal phase is stopped abruptly at the onset of menstruation each cycle.

subtopic_detail: Choosing between light therapy and pharmacotherapy in recurrent winter pattern depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a clinic in Hobart. A 29 year old woman has had four episodes of low mood, each beginning in late May and remitting by early October, with full return to normal function over summer in every year. She is now three weeks into this year's episode.

During episodes she sleeps ten hours and still feels unrefreshed, craves carbohydrate and has gained 5 kg each winter. She has never had an episode outside these months, has never been elevated, and there is no seasonal shift work or travel. She responded to sertraline two winters ago but stopped it because of sexual side effects and says she will not take it again. Her thyroid function and full blood count are normal, and her vitamin D is 58 nmol per litre.

data_table.Examination: Mildly slowed speech, reactive affect, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count within normal limits; serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D 58 nmol/L (50-150)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to recommend?

options.text: Prescribe high dose vitamin D supplementation and review her mood again in six weeks
options.rationale: Vitamin D supplementation has not shown antidepressant benefit in trials and her level is already within the reference range, so this delays effective treatment (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Start bright light therapy each morning with review of her response after two weeks
options.rationale: Morning bright light is a first line treatment for winter pattern depression with response rates comparable to antidepressants within one to two weeks, and it avoids the adverse effect that caused her to stop medication (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders; BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder

options.text: Start lithium as a mood stabiliser given the regular recurrence of her mood episodes
options.rationale: Regular recurrence is not bipolarity, and lithium is not indicated without a history of elevated mood or of recurrent depression resistant to standard treatment (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Restart sertraline at the dose that worked before and manage the side effects as they arise
options.rationale: Re prescribing an agent the patient has explicitly declined for a tolerability reason predicts poor adherence, and an equally effective alternative without that effect is available (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders).

options.text: Start agomelatine at night and review her sleep pattern and mood again in four weeks
options.rationale: Agomelatine has a melatonergic mechanism of theoretical appeal here but weaker evidence in this pattern, and it requires liver function monitoring that light therapy does not (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Depression with a seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depression when episodes begin and remit at characteristic times of year across at least two consecutive years, with seasonal episodes substantially outnumbering non seasonal ones over the lifetime. The winter pattern is distinguished by atypical features, namely hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving and weight gain, in contrast to the insomnia and weight loss of melancholic depression. Bright light therapy delivered in the morning is first line with efficacy comparable to antidepressants and a response typically evident within one to two weeks, and its main adverse effects are headache, eye strain and occasional switching to elevated mood in people with bipolar disorder. Latitude matters in Australia, and the condition is meaningfully more prevalent in Tasmania than in the tropical north, which is worth remembering when a patient's episodes track their move south.
key_points: The specifier requires a seasonal pattern across at least two consecutive years
Hypersomnia, carbohydrate craving and weight gain define the winter pattern
Morning bright light therapy is first line and works within one to two weeks
Screen for a bipolar history because light can precipitate elevated mood
Prevalence rises with latitude and is higher in Tasmania than in northern Australia
explanation.pearls: Bright light therapy is delivered as 10000 lux for about 30 minutes within an hour of waking, and shifting the session to the evening loses most of the benefit because the phase advancing effect depends on morning timing.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Seasonal Affective Disorder

subtopic_detail: Acute assessment of volatile substance use in an adolescent and the hazard of catecholamine provocation
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 15 year old boy is brought in by ambulance after being found in a park unsteady, giggling and slurring his words. Paramedics found aerosol cans nearby and noted a chemical smell on his breath. Twenty minutes later he is drowsy but rousable and oriented.

There is a rash of small red spots around his mouth and nose and his clothing smells of solvent. His breath alcohol is zero and a urine drug screen is negative for amphetamines, opioids, benzodiazepines and cannabis. He becomes agitated when the nursing staff try to attach the monitoring leads and wants to leave. His mother has been contacted and is on her way.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112, blood pressure 124/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Perioral erythematous rash, solvent odour, dysarthria and gait ataxia, pupils 4 mm and reactive, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Breath alcohol zero; urine drug screen negative; capillary glucose 5.4 mmol/L (4.0-7.8); electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with normal QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular droperidol for the agitation and repeat the dose if he remains unsettled
options.rationale: Sedation for agitation is standard in many intoxications, but here calm handling comes first because the myocardium is sensitised and both the struggle and the drug add cardiac risk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation and reassess his conscious state
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation, and the screen is negative while the clinical picture and odour point to an inhaled hydrocarbon (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Give activated charcoal now and admit him to the short stay unit for overnight observation
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind inhaled volatile hydrocarbons and adds aspiration risk in a drowsy patient (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Nurse him calmly in a quiet area with cardiac monitoring and supplemental oxygen as needed
options.rationale: Inhaled hydrocarbons sensitise the myocardium to catecholamines so that fright or exertion can precipitate ventricular arrhythmia, and minimising stimulation with cardiac monitoring is the specific management (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology; Poisons Information Centre Australia).

options.text: Discharge him to his mother once he is fully alert with advice to see his own doctor
options.rationale: Discharge without a period of monitoring, a review of the electrolytes and renal function and a plan for follow up misses both the cardiac window and the chance to intervene (Source: Poisons Information Centre Australia).

explanation.summary: Volatile substance use, most often of butane, propane and toluene from aerosols, lighter refills and glues, produces a rapid alcohol like intoxication that clears within an hour or two, so the diagnosis rests on the history, the solvent odour and the perioral rash rather than on a drug screen, which does not detect these agents. The critical pharmacology is that these hydrocarbons sensitise the myocardium to endogenous catecholamines, so a surge of adrenaline from a struggle, a fright or physical restraint can precipitate ventricular fibrillation, a phenomenon known as sudden sniffing death. Management is therefore deliberately low stimulus, with quiet nursing, cardiac monitoring and oxygen, and physical restraint and sympathomimetic drugs avoided wherever possible. Chronic use causes cerebellar and cognitive damage, a distal renal tubular acidosis with hypokalaemia from toluene, and bone marrow suppression from benzene, so electrolytes, renal function and a full blood count are checked and follow up arranged.
key_points: Routine urine drug screens do not detect volatile hydrocarbons
Perioral rash and solvent odour are the practical diagnostic clues
The myocardium is sensitised to catecholamines so fright or struggle can be fatal
Manage with quiet surroundings, cardiac monitoring and oxygen rather than restraint
Chronic use causes cerebellar damage, renal tubular acidosis and marrow suppression
explanation.pearls: Avoid adrenaline and other sympathomimetics in a patient who has inhaled hydrocarbons unless the patient is in arrest, because the sensitised myocardium responds to catecholamine with ventricular fibrillation.

subtopic_detail: Atypical features in a first psychotic presentation that redirect the workup away from a primary disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 21 year old woman admitted three days ago with a two week history of paranoid beliefs about her housemates, disorganised speech and severe anxiety. She has no personal or family psychiatric history and uses no substances, and a urine drug screen is negative.

Over the last 48 hours the nursing staff report she has become intermittently mute and then floridly agitated within the same hour. She has developed repetitive lip smacking and choreiform movements of both hands that were not present on admission and that persist during sleep observation. She has been febrile to 38.2 twice without a source, and her pulse has swung between 48 and 140 while lying still in bed. She has received two doses of olanzapine only.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate fluctuating 48 to 140, blood pressure 96/58 to 158/94, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Examination: Orofacial dyskinesia and hand chorea persisting in sleep, fluctuating conscious state, no neck stiffness, no rigidity or clonus
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0); C-reactive protein 9 mg/L (less than 5); creatine kinase 210 U/L (less than 200); urine drug screen negative; computed tomography of the brain reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease olanzapine and start bromocriptine with active cooling and intravenous fluid support
options.rationale: That is the treatment for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, whose defining features are lead pipe rigidity and a markedly raised creatine kinase, neither of which is present after only two doses (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Increase the olanzapine dose and add regular lorazepam for the fluctuating agitation
options.rationale: Escalating antipsychotic treats the presentation as primary psychosis and risks marked sensitivity reactions in autoimmune encephalitis, while the movement disorder and autonomic instability go uninvestigated (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis).

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture with paired serum and cerebrospinal fluid autoantibody testing
options.rationale: Subacute psychosis with orofacial dyskinesia, fluctuating conscious state, seizures or autonomic instability in a young woman requires testing for antibodies against the N methyl D aspartate receptor, and the cerebrospinal fluid sample is more sensitive than serum alone (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for a presumed catatonic presentation of psychosis
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is used for catatonia and is sometimes needed in this condition too, but committing to it before excluding an autoimmune cause bypasses the immunotherapy that alters the outcome (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis).

options.text: Start intravenous ceftriaxone and aciclovir empirically and repeat the computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Empirical cover for bacterial meningitis and herpes encephalitis is reasonable while awaiting the tap, but repeating a normal computed tomography scan adds nothing and does not substitute for the cerebrospinal fluid examination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Anti N methyl D aspartate receptor encephalitis characteristically begins with a prodrome of headache and fever followed by psychiatric symptoms, so a substantial proportion of patients are admitted to a psychiatric unit before the diagnosis is made. The features that should redirect the workup are a subacute onset over days to weeks in someone with no psychiatric history, a movement disorder that is typically orofacial dyskinesia and persists into sleep, a fluctuating conscious state, seizures, and autonomic instability with swings in heart rate, blood pressure and temperature. Diagnosis rests on antibody testing in cerebrospinal fluid as well as serum, since cerebrospinal fluid is considerably more sensitive and serum alone can be falsely negative, supported by magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography. Treatment is immunotherapy with corticosteroid, immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, escalating to rituximab or cyclophosphamide, together with a search for an underlying ovarian teratoma, and outcomes are markedly better the earlier treatment begins.
key_points: Subacute psychosis with no psychiatric history should prompt an organic workup
Orofacial dyskinesia persisting into sleep is close to specific for this condition
Autonomic instability and fluctuating conscious state are core supporting features
Cerebrospinal fluid antibody testing is more sensitive than serum alone
Search for an ovarian teratoma in young women once the diagnosis is made
explanation.pearls: Patients with anti N methyl D aspartate receptor encephalitis show marked sensitivity to antipsychotics, and a severe extrapyramidal or malignant syndrome type reaction after one or two ordinary doses is itself a diagnostic clue.

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid timing and eye protection in acute unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 38 year old man woke 30 hours ago unable to move the left side of his face. He noticed his coffee dribbling out of the left corner of his mouth and that his left eye waters constantly and feels gritty.

He cannot raise the left eyebrow or bury the left eyelashes, and the left eye rolls upwards when he attempts to close it. Taste is reduced on the left front of the tongue and sounds seem uncomfortably loud in the left ear. Limb power, coordination and reflexes are normal, the other cranial nerves are intact, and there is no rash or vesicle on the pinna, in the canal or on the palate. The tympanic membranes are normal and there is no parotid mass.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 15, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Complete left upper and lower facial weakness with positive Bell phenomenon, normal tympanic membranes, no vesicles, no parotid mass, no other cranial nerve deficit
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.6 mmol/L (4.0-7.8); no imaging performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral prednisolone now with lubricating drops by day and ointment plus taping at night
options.rationale: Corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset significantly improves the chance of complete recovery, and an eye that will not close needs mechanical protection to prevent exposure keratopathy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Start oral valaciclovir alone with lubricating drops and review the weakness in one week
options.rationale: Antiviral monotherapy does not improve outcomes, and antivirals are only ever considered as an addition to corticosteroid in severe or complete palsy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before starting any treatment for him
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for slowly progressive weakness, other cranial nerve involvement, forehead sparing or no recovery by three months, and obtaining it now would push him past the steroid window (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain to exclude a stroke as the cause of this
options.rationale: A supranuclear lesion spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation of the upper face, and forehead involvement here places the lesion in the lower motor neurone pathway (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer for facial nerve decompression surgery and start lubricating drops while he waits
options.rationale: Surgical decompression remains unproven, carries a hearing loss risk and is not part of routine management of an acute idiopathic palsy (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Idiopathic facial nerve palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion made on an acute unilateral lower motor neurone weakness involving the forehead, without other cranial nerve or long tract signs. Forehead involvement is the pivotal examination finding, because the upper face receives bilateral cortical input and is therefore spared in a stroke, while hyperacusis and altered taste localise the lesion proximally within the facial canal and support the diagnosis rather than arguing against it. Oral corticosteroid started within 72 hours of onset increases the proportion who recover completely, and the evidence for adding an antiviral is weak and reserved for severe or complete palsy. Eye care is the part most often neglected and the part most likely to cause lasting harm, since an eye that cannot close and has lost its protective reflex is at risk of corneal ulceration within days.
key_points: Forehead involvement distinguishes a lower motor neurone palsy from a stroke
Start oral corticosteroid within 72 hours of symptom onset
Antivirals are adjunctive at best and are not used alone
Lubrication by day and ointment with taping at night prevent exposure keratopathy
Vesicles in the canal or on the palate indicate herpes zoster oticus instead
explanation.pearls: No recovery at all by three months should prompt magnetic resonance imaging of the facial nerve, since a slowly enlarging parotid or nerve sheath tumour can present as what appears to be an ordinary palsy.

subtopic_detail: Bedside positional testing to separate peripheral positional vertigo from continuous vestibular loss
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 58 year old woman describes the room spinning when she rolls over in bed or tips her head back to hang washing. Each attack lasts under a minute and settles completely if she keeps still, and she is entirely well between attacks.

This has happened many times over the last three weeks. She has no hearing loss, tinnitus or ear fullness, and no headache, diplopia, dysarthria or limb symptoms. On the Dix Hallpike manoeuvre to the right there is a two second latency then upbeating torsional nystagmus lasting about 20 seconds with reproduction of her vertigo, and the manoeuvre to the left is negative. Gait is steady, the head impulse test is normal in both directions and there is no nystagmus at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72, blood pressure 132/80 lying and 128/78 standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Right Dix Hallpike positive with latency, upbeating torsional nystagmus and fatigability; normal head impulse test; no spontaneous nystagmus; normal cerebellar examination
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed in the practice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe prochlorperazine regularly for two weeks and review her symptoms afterwards
options.rationale: Vestibular sedatives suppress symptoms briefly but do not clear the displaced otoconia and delay central compensation, so regular use is discouraged (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Perform an Epley repositioning manoeuvre on the right side at this consultation today
options.rationale: Brief positionally triggered vertigo with a positive right Dix Hallpike showing latency, torsional upbeating nystagmus and fatigue identifies posterior canal otoconia, and repositioning resolves it in most patients in one or two attempts (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start a course of oral prednisolone and refer her for vestibular rehabilitation therapy
options.rationale: Corticosteroid and rehabilitation belong to vestibular neuritis, in which vertigo is continuous for days with an abnormal head impulse test rather than positionally triggered and brief (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the posterior fossa before treating her at all
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for direction changing or downbeating nystagmus, an abnormal neurological examination or a normal head impulse test with continuous vertigo, none of which fits this pattern (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Advise a low salt diet with betahistine and review the frequency of her attacks in six weeks
options.rationale: Salt restriction and betahistine are used in Meniere disease, whose distinguishing features are attacks lasting 20 minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

explanation.summary: Vertigo is best sorted by timing and triggers rather than by the quality of the sensation the patient describes. Episodes lasting seconds to a minute provoked reliably by a change in head position, with the patient entirely well in between, indicate otoconial debris in a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal on the affected side. The Dix Hallpike manoeuvre confirms it by reproducing the vertigo with a brief latency, torsional upbeating nystagmus and fatigue on repetition, and the Epley manoeuvre treats it in the same consultation with success in the majority. The main alternatives are vestibular neuritis, which gives days of continuous vertigo with an abnormal head impulse test, Meniere disease with attacks of 20 minutes to hours plus cochlear symptoms, and a posterior circulation stroke, which is suggested by direction changing or downbeating nystagmus, a normal head impulse test despite continuous vertigo, or any other neurological sign.
key_points: Sort vertigo by episode duration and trigger before considering the sensation itself
Positional attacks under a minute with a positive Dix Hallpike indicate canal otoconia
Latency, torsional upbeating nystagmus and fatigability confirm a peripheral cause
Treat with the Epley manoeuvre rather than with vestibular sedatives
Direction changing or downbeating nystagmus demands posterior fossa imaging
explanation.pearls: A normal head impulse test in a patient with continuous rather than positional vertigo is a red flag for stroke, because an intact vestibulo ocular reflex means the peripheral apparatus is working and the lesion lies centrally.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing conservative treatment and nerve conduction testing in nocturnal hand paraesthesia
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 47 year old woman who works as a hairdresser describes tingling and burning in her right hand that wakes her most nights and that she relieves by hanging the hand over the side of the bed and shaking it. It has been going on for five months.

The symptoms involve the thumb, index and middle fingers and spare the little finger, and she has begun dropping her scissors. Tapping over the front of the wrist reproduces the tingling and holding both wrists flexed for a minute brings it on within 30 seconds. There is no wasting of the thenar eminence and thumb abduction power is normal. Neck movements are full and painless and do not reproduce the symptoms, and reflexes in both arms are normal.

data_table.Examination: Reduced light touch over the radial three and a half digits, positive Tinel and Phalen signs at the right wrist, no thenar wasting, normal abductor pollicis brevis power, full painless cervical movements
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and glycated haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for surgical decompression of the affected nerve at the wrist within the next month
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated for thenar wasting, weakness of thumb abduction, constant sensory loss or failure of conservative treatment, and none of those applies with normal power and bulk (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine to look for nerve root compression
options.rationale: A cervical radiculopathy is the near diagnosis but it produces neck pain, reflex change and a dermatomal rather than nerve territory distribution, and neck movement is painless here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Fit a neutral position night splint and arrange nerve conduction studies to confirm severity
options.rationale: Nocturnal splinting in a neutral wrist position relieves symptoms in the majority without weakness, and nerve conduction testing grades severity and guides the decision about later surgery (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Prescribe a two week course of oral corticosteroid and review her symptoms after that time
options.rationale: Short oral corticosteroid gives modest and temporary relief and is used when splinting fails or as a bridge to surgery rather than as an initial treatment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Prescribe amitriptyline at a neuropathic pain dose and review her symptoms in four weeks
options.rationale: Neuropathic agents do not address the mechanical compression that is driving the symptoms and have not shown benefit in this entrapment (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy and the history alone is usually diagnostic, with nocturnal paraesthesia in the radial three and a half digits relieved by shaking the hand. The examination questions that matter are whether the little finger is involved, which would suggest a lesion elsewhere, and whether there is thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction, which indicates axonal loss and changes the management. Conservative treatment with a neutral wrist night splint helps most patients without motor involvement, and nerve conduction studies grade severity, confirm the diagnosis when it is uncertain and are generally required before surgical referral. Secondary contributors worth screening for include hypothyroidism, diabetes, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis and acromegaly, since treating them can resolve the entrapment.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesia relieved by shaking the hand is the classic history
Sparing of the little finger keeps the lesion at the wrist rather than higher up
Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction indicates axonal loss and prompts surgery
Neutral position night splinting is effective first line conservative treatment
Screen for thyroid disease, diabetes, pregnancy and inflammatory arthritis
explanation.pearls: Splint the wrist in neutral rather than in extension, since a wrist extension splint raises carpal tunnel pressure and is a frequent reason a patient reports that splinting made the symptoms worse.

subtopic_detail: Positive diagnosis of a functional bowel disorder versus reflex endoscopy in a young adult
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 27 year old woman has had lower abdominal cramping for two years that comes and goes, is relieved by opening her bowels, and alternates between loose stools three times a morning and two days without a motion. She feels bloated by the evening and better in the morning.

She has not lost weight, has never seen blood in the toilet or on the paper, and has no nocturnal symptoms that wake her from sleep. There is no family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Examination reveals mild left iliac fossa tenderness with no mass and a normal perianal inspection. Full blood count, C-reactive protein, coeliac serology on a gluten containing diet and faecal calprotectin are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, mild left iliac fossa tenderness without guarding, no palpable mass, normal perianal and rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-165); C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5); tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A negative with normal total immunoglobulin A; faecal calprotectin 22 mcg/g (less than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for colonoscopy to exclude inflammatory bowel disease before offering any treatment
options.rationale: Colonoscopy is indicated by alarm features or a raised calprotectin, and a normal calprotectin has a high negative predictive value for mucosal inflammation in this age group (Source: GESA: Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Make a positive diagnosis, explain the condition and trial dietary and symptom directed therapy
options.rationale: Symptom criteria are met with normal limited testing and no alarm features, so a confident positive diagnosis with explanation and a dietary trial is the recommended approach rather than further exclusion (Source: GESA: Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Advise a strict gluten free diet for three months and repeat the coeliac serology afterwards
options.rationale: Coeliac serology taken on a gluten containing diet with normal total immunoglobulin A has already excluded coeliac disease, and gluten withdrawal would invalidate any repeat testing (Source: GESA: Coeliac Disease).

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and intravenous contrast
options.rationale: Cross sectional imaging carries radiation exposure in a young woman and has very low yield when there are no alarm features and inflammatory markers are normal (Source: GESA: Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

options.text: Prescribe a proton pump inhibitor and an antispasmodic and review her symptoms in six weeks
options.rationale: An antispasmodic is a reasonable symptomatic agent but acid suppression has no role in lower abdominal symptoms, and prescribing without explaining the diagnosis misses the intervention with the largest effect (Source: GESA: Irritable Bowel Syndrome).

explanation.summary: Irritable bowel syndrome is diagnosed positively on recurrent abdominal pain related to defaecation or associated with a change in stool frequency or form, rather than by excluding everything else. In a young patient with no alarm features the workup is deliberately limited to a full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin, and normal results in that panel make significant organic disease very unlikely. Alarm features that redirect towards endoscopy are age over 50 at onset, rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, a family history of bowel cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and a palpable mass. A confident explanation of the diagnosis is itself therapeutic, and is followed by dietary modification, soluble fibre, an antispasmodic for pain, and consideration of a low dose tricyclic or gut directed psychological therapy where symptoms persist.
key_points: Diagnose positively on symptom criteria rather than by exhaustive exclusion
Limited testing means full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology and calprotectin
Normal faecal calprotectin makes inflammatory bowel disease very unlikely
Alarm features include age over 50, bleeding, weight loss and nocturnal symptoms
A clear explanation of the diagnosis is an active part of treatment
explanation.pearls: A low fermentable carbohydrate diet should be supervised by a dietitian and formally reintroduced after six to eight weeks, since indefinite restriction narrows the diet and reduces the beneficial colonic microbiota.

subtopic_detail: Recognition of an emergent spinal syndrome in a patient with a long history of mechanical back pain
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 44 year old warehouse worker with ten years of intermittent mechanical low back pain presents at 11 pm with three days of much worse pain radiating down both legs after lifting a pallet.

He has passed no urine since the morning and says he does not feel any urge, although he has not felt his bladder full either. He mentions in passing that the toilet seat felt strange against his skin this evening. Straight leg raise is limited to 40 degrees bilaterally, ankle jerks are absent on both sides and there is reduced sensation to light touch across both buttocks and the inner thighs. Power is 4 out of 5 in ankle plantarflexion bilaterally. He is afebrile, has never been diagnosed with cancer and does not inject drugs. A bladder scan shows a residual volume of 780 mL.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 138/82, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Bilateral reduced perineal sensation, absent ankle jerks, plantarflexion power 4 of 5 bilaterally, reduced anal tone on rectal examination
data_table.Investigations: Bladder ultrasound post void residual 780 mL; C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Insert a urinary catheter and arrange emergency magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine tonight
options.rationale: Bilateral radicular pain with saddle sensory loss, reduced anal tone and painless retention is a compressive cauda equina syndrome, and imaging within hours determines whether decompression can preserve continence (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome

options.text: Give opioid analgesia with diazepam and arrange an outpatient magnetic resonance scan this week
options.rationale: Treating this as a severe episode of his usual mechanical pain delays decompression, and the window in which sphincter function can be preserved is measured in hours (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome

options.text: Start high dose intravenous dexamethasone and arrange a computed tomography scan of the spine
options.rationale: Corticosteroid and computed tomography belong to suspected malignant cord compression, and he has no cancer history, no fever and normal inflammatory markers (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome

options.text: Arrange plain lumbar spine radiographs and refer him to the physiotherapy clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: Plain films do not show neural compression and physiotherapy referral treats this as ordinary back pain despite objective sphincter and saddle findings (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Start empirical intravenous antibiotics and take blood cultures to cover a spinal infection
options.rationale: Epidural abscess is the important infective mimic but it presents with fever, raised inflammatory markers and often a source such as injecting drug use, none of which is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Cauda equina syndrome is the one back pain presentation where hours matter, and it is missed because the patient usually has a long history of ordinary mechanical pain that makes the new episode look like more of the same. The features to elicit actively are bilateral radicular symptoms, saddle or perineal sensory change, reduced anal tone, and bladder dysfunction, which begins as loss of the sensation of filling and progresses to painless retention with overflow rather than to obvious inability to void. Painless retention with a large residual volume is late rather than early, so the earlier symptoms of reduced urinary sensation and altered perineal feeling are the ones that buy time. Urgent magnetic resonance imaging is the investigation, and surgical decompression as soon as possible after diagnosis gives the best chance of preserving continence and sexual function, with delay strongly associated with permanent deficit.
key_points: A long history of mechanical back pain does not protect against this diagnosis
Ask directly about perineal sensation and the sensation of bladder filling
Painless retention with a large residual is a late sign, not an early one
Magnetic resonance imaging is required urgently, not electively
Delay to decompression correlates with permanent bladder and sexual dysfunction
explanation.pearls: Loss of the sensation of urinary flow passing through the urethra is one of the earliest symptoms of cauda equina compression and appears well before painless retention, so it is worth asking about by name.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Cauda Equina Syndrome
